title: playdough
status_note: Contract, research and a landing page exist; the generator itself is not built.
oneliner: Turns one sentence into a small game you can play from a link.
role: I wrote the intent, the research behind it and the landing page, and I am steering the visual direction.

media.alt: playdough landing page at desktop width
media.caption: The landing page, built from the Secret Sauce house style.

media.alt: Rendered isometric game diorama from the visuals worktree
media.caption: A render from the visuals worktree: the look a generated game should have.
One of six vignettes, frog pond, used to test the pixel and ink-edge look.

body: The goal: a stranger types one sentence and plays the result from a link, with a 20-second clip to share. That is the target, not a result. Today playdough is a contract, four research notes and a landing page.

It is a generator, not an engine. It sits on templates from mise_en_place and a design-brief step that turns a vague idea into a fun core loop before anything is built. A human playtest comes before anything is shared.
So far the useful work has been visual: six rendered vignettes testing whether generated art can look deliberate. I learned to settle the look before the pipeline.

title: Mise en Place
status_note: Intent, landing page and a manual are written; the prep-pack tool is not built.
oneliner: Preps a ready game project from one sentence, so the agent skips setup.
role: I defined the prep-pack idea, wrote the intent and the landing page, and drew its look.

hero.alt: Mise en Place title card, prepped bowls on a tray

media.caption: The landing page: research, assets and references laid out before the cooking starts.
The portrait card, one of the generated social assets.

spec.label: parts in a pack
spec.source: site/copy.md: research, generated assets, references, an indexed folder

body: The target: give it one sentence about a game and it lays out a prep pack on disk, with a chosen template, an asset kit, a context brief and a manifest, before the agent starts. Zero setup steps for the agent is the goal. The tool does not exist yet.
What exists is the intent, a landing page, a manual, and a short list of lessons borrowed from my earlier research repos, including one finding that packing evidence loses more than searching for it.
I learned to write down what a tool is not. It is not an agent harness and not the decision model.

title: bonfire
status_note: Intent, a fork-base decision and a landing page; no harness code of its own yet.
oneliner: Runs AI agents until the work passes your checks, even through a crash.
role: I wrote the intent and the fork-base decision, and I am reusing the loop design from my older gauntlet repo.

hero.alt: bonfire title card, a flame over crossed logs

media.caption: The landing page: the loop, the queued tasks and four worker lanes.

spec.label: old-repo tests inherited as reference
spec.source: salvage-summary.md: gauntlet, 67 tests pass (reference only, no code moved)

body: The target: one propose, evaluate, critique, verify loop fans out four parallel workers on a real task, and the run survives a forced restart. That demo has not run. bonfire is an intent file, a decision to build on an existing harness, and a landing page.
The loop itself comes from gauntlet, a small Python harness I built earlier. I am carrying its phases and its resume design as reference, not its code. See the old repos entry.
I learned that a harness needs durable state first, because model calls fail and long runs get killed.

title: nibble
status_note: Experiments on a branch; the decider is not packaged or measured against a big model.
oneliner: Answers an agent's multiple-choice questions fast and says how sure it is.
role: I wrote the intent, run the experiments, and studied what my earlier classifier attempts got wrong.

body: The target: a small model that picks among typed options in an agent pipeline, returns calibrated odds, and beats a big model on speed. It builds on Kev, an open model, rather than replacing it. Speed and accuracy claims are not measured yet.
The first experiment has Kev-4B compose shadcn landing pages, then a fine-tune on rubric labels on my shared 3060. It is exploratory and lives on a branch.
My earlier classifiers taught me the most: one scored 44.5% on unseen wording at 97% confidence. Calibration on new phrasing is the real test.

body: The target: an agent and I edit one component on a canvas at once, and the result is a real component file on disk. In the spikes, the two-cursor demo runs; it is not a product and I have not used it for real work.

napkin is the latest part of the plan, so the spikes are deliberately small and in separate worktrees. The spec borrows a short list of invariants from my earlier precision-canvas repo and leaves its spec behind.
I learned to start from the file format, because files on disk stay the source of truth.

title: The old repos
status_note: Salvage audit, read-only; no old code was moved.
oneliner: Five earlier AI repos, audited for what the kitchen keeps.
role: I audited my own earlier repos for the kitchen: what to carry as a reference excerpt, and what to leave.

hero.alt: Bonfire plate: a flame glyph with callouts

media.alt: Bar chart: 73 required paragraphs, 70 found by search, 54 packed into the model
media.caption: From local-mobile-research: evidence is lost after it is found, so allocation is the problem, not recall.
The lmr app from the same repo.

body: I audited my earlier repos before building the kitchen. The default verdict was to leave. Nothing was copied wholesale; only excerpts with a provenance note moved into the new repos' reference docs.
gauntlet: a Python harness for propose, evaluate, critique, verify over git worktrees, with resume. Its loop and store design go to bonfire. It was never measured on real model runs.

system-a and system-one-mini: classifier experiments. system-a drifted into labeling a coding agent's next tool. system-one-mini was fast (4.95 ms p50) but scored 44.5% on unseen wording at 97% confidence and its final 86% held only in-domain. I carry those failures into nibble, not the code.

precision-canvas: meant as a component canvas, it became a spec programme with 473 capabilities and no editor. napkin takes a few invariants and checklists. local-mobile-research: an offline QA tournament whose lesson, that packing loses evidence rather than retrieval, goes to mise_en_place.
